Take-Two (TTWO) jumped 8% as Grand Theft Auto VI launched, but the gain partly rebounds a 10% slide in the two days before release.

Communication Services Select Sector SPDR (XLC) carries a 5% Take-Two weight, so the launch moves it far more than Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), at 0.2%.

Overlapping Nasdaq-100, sector, and gaming funds stack exposure to one launch, so investors may own Take-Two several times over without choosing it.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Shares of Take-Two Interactive (NASDAQ:TTWO) rose 8.39% to $221.04 as of 11:42 AM ET Wednesday as Grand Theft Auto VI began its global launch. Reuters and CNBC reported that the stock jumped as gamers enjoyed the blockbuster release, and CNBC noted shares had climbed more than 6% in premarket trading on glowing reviews from critics and players. Business Insider reported reviews calling the game a "masterpiece," while Barron's reported stellar reviews. Yahoo Finance reported that preorders topped $1.65 billion, a figure Take-Two has not confirmed.

AJerArt / Shutterstock.com
TTWO Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

For retirement savers, the more practical question is where they already own this stock. Take-Two appears inside several widely held ETFs, and a launch-day move flows through each one in proportion to its weight.

Today's Gain Follows a Pre-Launch Slide

Part of today's move is a rebound. A 24/7 Wall St. report published Wednesday said Take-Two lost 10% in the two days before launch. Even after today's gain, shares are down 1.6% over the past week and 13.67% year to date.

Last quarter's results explain some of the caution. Fiscal second-quarter revenue of $1.497 billion missed the $1.656 billion consensus and fell 15.6% year over year, and the company posted a GAAP loss of $0.29 per share. One strong session is a reaction to launch-day reviews; whether it becomes a turnaround depends on sales data still to come.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

It has been a loud stretch for markets. On Nov 12, Nvidia said Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO. Inflation ran hot enough to firm up bets on a Fed rate hike in December. And the Anthropic IPO is expected to price tonight.

Your brokerage statement may tell a quieter story. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF, SCHD, is up 31.9% this year through Nov 17, with dividends included. Only 2013 was better, at 32.9%. So 2026 is, so far, the fund's best calendar year since 2013.

The broad market did far less. The S&P 500 fund SPY rose 8.2%, and the Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ rose 7.3%. The health care fund XLV rose 21.1%. The consumer staples fund XLP, which holds makers of everyday goods, rose 20.0%. The other big dividend funds, VYM, DVY, DGRO and SDY, rose 14.3% to 18.2%. In a year when AI stocks wobbled, the steady dividend payers came out ahead. SCHD beat the S&P 500 fund by about 24 points.

That gap can change your mix on its own. If you own both kinds of fund, your mix has tilted toward dividend stocks without a single trade.

If steady dividend payers carried your year, you may want a fuller set of them. The Trefis Income Solution holds 50 dividend stocks yielding about 3x the S&P 500, each with at least 10 straight years of dividends. It lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the Income Solution.

What Came The Year After A Big Year?

SCHD's three best years before this one were 2013, 2021 and 2019. In the years after, it returned +11.7%, −3.3% and +15.0%. The worst of the three was that 3.3% loss. The middle result was a gain of 11.7%.

We widened the test to other dividend funds: DVY (since 2004), SDY, VYM and DGRO. We also added the staples fund XLP (since 2008). Across them all, a fund rose 25% or more in a calendar year 13 times. All 13 cases fall in just three years.

Bank of America Has a Message for Chip Stock Investors
Moz Farooque ACCA

BAC

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Betting on semiconductor stocks is still the market's most crowded trade, according to Bank of America's November Global Fund Manager Survey.

But only 39% of respondents put it at the top, down from 82% in July. The trade has held its No. 1 ranking even as the share of managers who see it as the most crowded has more than halved.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with GS.

Is QQQ fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The next closest trades were betting against Chinese equities, cited by 14% of respondents, and betting on the Magnificent Seven, at 12%. The survey ran from Nov. 6 to 12 and covered 193 panelists managing $526 billion.

The survey also found that managers made their biggest cut to technology overweights since 2006. Meanwhile, 52% expect a major cloud provider to announce a capital spending cut within six months, up from 30% in October.

An AI bubble was the most frequently cited market tail risk, at 34%, followed by a credit event at a major cloud provider, at 31%.

Investors Takeaway

The drop from 82% to 39% measures how managers rank the trade's crowding. The survey's technology allocation figures show that managers reduced exposure to the broader sector, while the size of any pullback from chip stocks specifically remains unclear.

The next test is what cloud providers say about their spending plans. A cut could weaken expectations for future chip orders while semiconductors still top the crowding rankings.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Nvidia reported after Tuesday's close. Revenue was $115.8 billion in the three months to Oct 25, up 103% from a year ago. The midpoint of its guidance for next quarter's revenue is $130.0 billion. The usual question is whether the quarter was good enough. This article asks a different question. How much Nvidia do index fund owners already hold, and what would a deep fall cost them?

A $1,000,000 portfolio split evenly between VOO and QQQ holds about $61,705 of Nvidia. That is 6.2% of the whole portfolio. Nvidia has had seven falls of 50% or more since 1999. A repeat of any of them on that slice would cost between $32,036 and $55,363 through Nvidia alone.

This holder has already lost money on Nvidia since October. Nvidia closed at $155.46 on Tuesday. That is 35.0% below its 2026 high close of $239.24 on Oct 6. The same Nvidia shares inside the two funds were worth about $33,254 more at that high.

Where The Nvidia Stake Comes From

VOO tracks the S&P 500. In its latest holdings file on our platform, Nvidia is the largest of 519 holdings, at 8.4% of the fund. But that file prices each Nvidia share at $228.38, which was the Sep 30 close. Since then Nvidia has fallen 31.9%, while VOO fell about 4%. Rolled forward to Tuesday's close, Nvidia's weight in VOO is an estimated 5.9%.

QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100. Its file shows Nvidia at 6.8% of the fund, priced at the Nov 10 close of $168.89. Since then, Nvidia has fallen 8.0% and QQQ has fallen 2.6%. That puts Nvidia's estimated weight in QQQ at 6.4%.

So $500,000 in VOO holds about $29,729 of Nvidia. The same amount in QQQ holds about $31,976. If all $1,000,000 sat in VOO, the stake would be about $59,458. All in QQQ, it would be about $63,952.

These weights are estimates. They assume no index changes and no fund trading since each file's date. Using the files as published would show $75,771 of Nvidia, which overstates the stake after the recent fall. If you also own Nvidia shares directly, add that position dollar for dollar.

What Nvidia's Seven Deep Falls Would Cost

Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) released its November Global Fund Manager Survey on November 17, 2026. It shows the net share of managers overweight technology fell to 12% from 37% in October. That 25-point drop is the largest one-month drop since June 2006.

Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images

Tech is still a net overweight, and the survey measures how managers say they are allocated rather than what they traded. Between 169 and 193 managers managing $461 billion to $526 billion answered the global poll from November 6 to November 12.

Stocks fell on the release date. The S&P 500 dropped 1.03% to 7,340.53, its fourth straight lower close, down from 7,619.38 on November 11.

The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) closed lower at $163.26. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 0.73% to $656.95, and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) dropped 9.45% to $194.52.

Both funds rose after hours once NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) reported, with XLK at $166.78 and QQQ at $665.93. After-hours quotes can change before the open.

Managers Are Turning Against AI Spending

Now 52% of managers expect at least one AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut within six months, up from 30% in October. This forecast remains unconfirmed by any hyperscaler announcement.

title: When SPY Falls 10%, Do Treasury Bonds Still Help?

When SPY Falls 10%, Do Treasury Bonds Still Help?
Trefis Team

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Bonds have had a bad five years. IEF, a fund of 7- to 10-year Treasury bonds, lost 7.7% in total return over the five years to Tuesday, Nov 17. SPY, the S&P 500 fund, gained 67.3% over the same years. So one camp says the 60/40 mix of stocks and bonds is broken. The other says bonds are back because they now pay more.

This article asks a different question. When stocks fell hard, did bonds soften the blow? The answer is yes, mostly. In 8 of the 10 finished S&P 500 falls of 10% or more since Nov 2002, IEF rose while stocks fell. A 60/40 mix of SPY and IEF lost less than SPY alone in all 10 of them. That includes 2022.

The current fall is the newest entry in our table. SPY is down 6.0% from its Oct 6 closing high. That is short of the 10% line, so it is not a correction yet. Over the same weeks IEF is up 1.8%. The 60/40 mix has lost 48.1% of what SPY lost. That is right at the median of 48.8% in past falls.

This piece is part of our storyline on whether the 60/40 mix still works. Our five-year look at the mix measures the long-run return. This one measures the hedge inside each fall.

How We Counted Each Fall

A fall starts at a closing high for SPY and ends at its lowest close before it gets back to that high. It counts if SPY lost 10% or more in total return, with dividends included. The 60/40 mix is bought at the high and held to the low. Nobody rebalances along the way.

The 2023 dip just misses. SPY fell 10.3% on price but less than 10% with dividends. So it is not in the table. The 1999 and 2000-2002 falls have no bond fund data in our prices, so those rows show stocks only.
